topics: Appendix A.1, printed p. 328; PDF p. 348 — Purpose and scope of the linear-algebra review: only the matrix terms and properties used in the main text, with proofs and motivation for most results.

Appendix A.2, printed pp. 328–330; PDF pp. 348–350 — Range/column space, row space, null space, four notions of rank, rank deficiency/full rank/nonsingularity, and rank under multiplication and sums of outer products.

Appendix A.3.1, printed pp. 330–333; PDF pp. 350–353 — General-matrix eigenpairs, characteristic equation, similarity, trace and determinant identities, |I−AB|=|I−BA|, and shared nonzero eigenvalues of AB and BA.

Appendix A.3.2, printed pp. 333–336; PDF pp. 353–356 — Hermitian eigenvalue decomposition, real eigenvalues, orthonormal eigenvectors, Rayleigh quotient, and extended trace/Rayleigh bounds for semiunitary subspaces.

Appendix A.4, printed pp. 336–341; PDF pp. 356–361 — Singular value decomposition; bases for range and null spaces; orthogonal complements and projectors; idempotence; Frobenius norm; best fixed-rank approximation and uniqueness.

Appendix A.5, printed pp. 341–345; PDF pp. 361–365 — Equivalent definitions of positive semidefinite/definite matrices, matrix square roots and Cholesky factors, Hadamard-product positivity, a Schur-complement inequality, log-determinant differentiation, and Cauchy–Schwarz for vectors/functions.

Appendix A.6, printed pp. 345–347; PDF pp. 365–367 — Vandermonde, Toeplitz, Hankel, and exchange matrices; independence of consecutive Vandermonde rows; symmetry/skew-symmetry structure of symmetric-Toeplitz eigenvectors.
Appendix A.7, printed p. 347; PDF p. 367 — Partitioned-matrix inverse formulas and the matrix inversion lemma.

Appendix A.8.1, printed pp. 347–350; PDF pp. 367–370 — Consistent linear systems: range/rank consistency test, general solution, uniqueness, SVD minimum-norm solution, Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, numerical stability, and condition number.

Appendix A.8.2, printed pp. 350–353; PDF pp. 370–373 — Inconsistent systems: least squares as right-hand-side perturbation, projection and normal-equation formula, QR implementation, total least squares as perturbation of both A and B, and SVD solution/uniqueness.
Appendix A.9, printed pp. 353–354; PDF pp. 373–374 — Unconstrained and linearly constrained Hermitian quadratic minimization by completing the square.

Appendix B.1, printed pp. 355–358; PDF pp. 375–378 — Why Cramér–Rao bounds matter for spectral analysis; first-order propagation from parameter covariance to spectral MSE; finite- versus large-sample interpretation; ML efficiency; unknown-order penalty.
Appendix B.2, printed pp. 358–359; PDF pp. 378–379 — CRB for general distributions from the score covariance/Fisher information and equivalently the expected log-likelihood Hessian.

Appendix B.3, printed pp. 359–364; PDF pp. 379–384 — Real Gaussian Slepian–Bangs CRB; circular complex Gaussian representation and compact formula; Gaussian CRB as a broadly useful conservative benchmark.

Appendix B.4, printed pp. 364–365; PDF pp. 384–385 — CRB construction for sinusoidal line spectra, conditioning on phases, finite versus asymptotic bounds, random-phase/posterior variants, and colored/non-Gaussian extensions.

Appendix B.5, printed pp. 365–367; PDF pp. 385–387 — Exact and large-sample CRBs for ARMA/rational spectra; covariance derivatives as ARMA cross-covariances; prediction-error formulation that avoids N-dimensional matrices.

Appendix B.6, printed pp. 367–376; PDF pp. 387–396 — Spatial-spectrum/DOA CRBs under deterministic-signal and stochastic-signal array models; closed forms; relation between bounds; regularity failure from growing nuisance-parameter dimension; method-versus-assumption interpretation.
Appendix C.1, printed pp. 377–378; PDF pp. 397–398 — Model order as parameter dimension for ARMA, line spectra, and source enumeration; order-selection rules coupled to maximum likelihood.

Appendix C.2, printed pp. 378–381; PDF pp. 398–401 — Maximum likelihood, Gaussian reduction to nonlinear least squares and residual variance, asymptotic normality/information matrix, regularity conditions, and sinusoidal parameter counting.

Appendix C.3.1, printed pp. 381–384; PDF pp. 401–404 — Order selection as mutually exclusive hypothesis testing; nested/non-nested models; MAP rule and proof that it maximizes total probability of correct detection.
Appendix C.3.2, printed pp. 384–385; PDF pp. 404–405 — Kullback–Leibler discrepancy, nonnegativity/equality conditions, and information-loss interpretation.

key_results: Rank is simultaneously the dimension of the column space and row space and the size of the largest nonsingular minor; nonsingular pre- or postmultiplication preserves it, while rank(AB)≤min(rank A,rank B). [A.2, Results R1–R2, printed pp. 329–330; PDF pp. 349–350]
A sum of N outer products has rank at most min(m,N), and premultiplication by a full-column-rank matrix preserves the rank of the following factor. [A.2, Results R3–R4, printed p. 330; PDF p. 350]

Similarity transformations preserve eigenvalues; trace equals the sum of eigenvalues and is cyclic across a conformable two-factor product. [A.3.1, Results R6–R8, printed pp. 331–332; PDF pp. 351–352]
For conformable A and B, |I−AB|=|I−BA| and AB and BA share all nonzero eigenvalues, even when their dimensions differ. [A.3.1, Results R10–R11, printed p. 333; PDF p. 353]
A Hermitian matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, so A=UΛU*. [A.3.2, Result R12, printed p. 333; PDF p. 353]
The Rayleigh quotient v*Av/(v*v) lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalues of Hermitian A, with equality at the corresponding eigenvectors. [A.3.2, Result R13, printed p. 334; PDF p. 354]

For semiunitary V with n columns, tr(V*AV) lies between the sums of the n smallest and n largest eigenvalues; the extremizing subspaces are spanned by the associated eigenvectors. [A.3.2, Result R14, printed pp. 334–336; PDF pp. 354–356]

For rank-r A=U1Σ1V1*, U1 and V1 span the column and row spaces, while U2 and V2 span the complementary null spaces; dim N(A*)=m−r and dim N(A)=n−r. [A.4, Results R15–R16, printed pp. 336–338; PDF pp. 356–358]
The orthogonal projectors onto R(A) and N(A*) are Π=U1U1* and Π⊥=I−U1U1*=U2U2*. Projector eigenvalues are only zero or one. [A.4, Result R17 and Definition D10, printed pp. 338–339; PDF pp. 358–359]

Truncating the SVD to the p largest singular values gives the best rank-p approximation in Frobenius norm, with squared error Σ_(k>p)σ_k²; it is unique iff σ_p>σ_(p+1). [A.4, Result R18, printed pp. 339–341; PDF pp. 359–361]

Positive (semi)definiteness is equivalently characterized by nonnegative eigenvalues, nonnegative quadratic forms, factorization A=CC*, or principal-minor conditions. [A.5, Definition D11, printed pp. 341–342; PDF pp. 361–362]

A positive semidefinite matrix has infinitely many square roots; the positive semidefinite Hermitian square root is unique, and a positive-definite matrix has a unique Cholesky factor with nonnegative diagonal. [A.5, Definition D12, printed p. 342; PDF p. 362]
The Hadamard product of two positive semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite. [A.5, Result R19, printed pp. 342–343; PDF pp. 362–363]
If [[A,I],[I,B]] is positive semidefinite and B is nonsingular, then A−B^−1 is positive semidefinite. [A.5, Result R20, printed p. 343; PDF p. 363]
For differentiable positive-definite C(α), ∂ln|C|/∂α=tr(C^−1∂C/∂α), the identity repeatedly used in Gaussian likelihood calculations. [A.5, Result R21, printed pp. 343–344; PDF pp. 363–364]

Cauchy–Schwarz is derived from positivity of a 2×2 Gram matrix for both vectors and integrable functions; equality holds exactly for proportional arguments. [A.5, Results R22–R23, printed pp. 344–345; PDF pp. 364–365]
For distinct nonzero nodes and m≥n, any n consecutive rows of the m×n Vandermonde matrix are linearly independent. [A.6, Result R24, printed pp. 345–346; PDF pp. 365–366]
The block inverse/Schur-complement identities imply the matrix inversion lemma (A−CB^−1D)^−1=A^−1+A^−1C(B−DA^−1C)^−1DA^−1. [A.7, Results R26–R27, printed p. 347; PDF p. 367]
AX=B is consistent iff R(B)⊆R(A), equivalently rank([A B])=rank(A); it has a unique solution iff that holds and A has full column rank. [A.8.1, Results R28–R30, printed pp. 347–348; PDF pp. 367–368]

For a consistent rank-r system, A†=V1Σ1^−1U1* yields the unique minimum-Frobenius-norm solution X0=A†B; all other solutions add a component from N(A). [A.8.1, Result R31 and Definition D15, printed pp. 348–349; PDF pp. 368–369]
Solution sensitivity is governed by cond(A)=σ1/σn. A numerically stable algorithm can still return an inaccurate solution to an ill-conditioned problem. [A.8.1, printed pp. 349–350; PDF pp. 369–370]

For full-column-rank inconsistent AX≈B, the LS solution is (A*A)^−1A*B, but directly forming A*A squares the condition number; QR gives the more stable triangular solve RX=Q1*B. [A.8.2, Result R32, printed pp. 350–351; PDF pp. 370–371]

TLS minimizes perturbations in both A and B. If [A B] has the stated partitioned SVD, X_TLS=−Ṽ21Ṽ22^−1; uniqueness requires a singular-value gap σ̃_n>σ̃_(n+1). [A.8.2, Result R33, printed pp. 352–353; PDF pp. 372–373]
For Hermitian positive-definite A, the unconstrained quadratic F(X)=X*AX+X*B+B*X+C is uniquely minimized at X0=−A^−1B with F(X0)=C−B*A^−1B. [A.9, Result R34, printed pp. 353–354; PDF pp. 373–374]
The linearly constrained minimum of X*AX subject to X*B=C is X0=A^−1B(B*A^−1B)^−1C*. [A.9, Result R35, printed p. 354; PDF p. 374]

For a smooth parametric spectrum, first-order error propagation gives MSE[φ(ω,θ̂)]≈ψ^T(ω,θ)Pψ(ω,θ); parameter-covariance bounds therefore induce frequency-by-frequency spectral MSE bounds. [B.1, equations B.1.1–B.1.4, printed p. 355; PDF p. 375]

The standard CRB bounds covariance of unbiased estimators, but in finite samples it may be unattainable and biased estimators may have smaller MSE; its most persuasive benchmark role is asymptotic, where regular ML estimators attain it. [B.1, printed pp. 356–357; PDF pp. 376–377]

When order is estimated as well as continuous parameters, the large-sample spectral bound becomes an average of order-conditional bounds over Pr(n̂=n); increasing the maximum allowed order increases this error—the price of unknown model dimension. [B.1, equation B.1.10, printed pp. 357–358; PDF pp. 377–378]

For a general differentiable likelihood, P_CR=[E{ss^T}]^−1=−[E{∂²ln p/∂θ∂θ^T}]^−1, where s is the score, and every unbiased estimator satisfies P≥P_CR. [B.2, Result R36, printed pp. 358–359; PDF pp. 378–379]
For real Gaussian data with mean μ(θ) and covariance C(θ), the Slepian–Bangs formula is [P_CR^−1]_ij=(1/2)tr(C^−1C_i'C^−1C_j')+μ_i'^TC^−1μ_j'. [B.3, Result R37, printed pp. 359–361; PDF pp. 379–381]
For circular complex Gaussian data, the compact information element is tr(Γ^−1Γ_i'Γ^−1Γ_j')+2Re{μ_i'^*Γ^−1μ_j'}. [B.3, equation B.3.25, printed pp. 361–363; PDF pp. 381–383]

Under broad congruity/large-sample conditions, the Gaussian CRB is at least as large as the CRB under other distributions with the same mean/covariance; it is therefore a conservative lower-bound benchmark for many second-order methods, though non-Gaussian structure can in principle beat it. [B.3, equations B.3.26–B.3.27, printed pp. 363–364; PDF pp. 383–384]

For line spectra with deterministic phases in circular Gaussian white noise, mean is Vandermonde signal synthesis and covariance is σ²I; exact finite-N CRBs follow from Slepian–Bangs, while a simpler frequency bound is accurate when minimum separation exceeds roughly 1/N. [B.4, printed pp. 364–365; PDF pp. 384–385]

For ARMA models, exact CRB ingredients reduce to autocovariance and cross-covariance computations. The large-sample prediction-error form P_CR,θ={E[ΔΛ^−1Δ^T]}^−1 avoids inverses of matrices whose dimension grows with N. [B.5, equations B.5.5–B.5.6, printed pp. 365–367; PDF pp. 385–387]

For array DOA under deterministic unknown snapshots, CRB_Det(DOA)=σ²/(2N){Re[(D*Π_A⊥D)⊙P̂^T]}^−1; the stochastic-signal model replaces the second factor with one involving PA*R^−1AP. [B.6, equations B.6.32–B.6.33, printed p. 372; PDF p. 392]

With sample signal covariance converging to P, the DOA bounds obey CRB_Sto(DOA)≥CRB_Det(DOA), but they arise from different full data models and only their DOA blocks are meaningfully compared. [B.6, equations B.6.34–B.6.39, printed pp. 372–373; PDF pp. 392–393]

ML under the deterministic-snapshot array model need not attain CRB_Det because the nuisance-parameter count grows with N; ML under the stochastic model satisfies standard fixed-dimension efficiency conditions. [B.6, printed pp. 373–374; PDF pp. 393–394]

Under Gaussian white noise y=μ(γ)+e, ML reduces to NLS: γ̂ minimizes ||y−μ(γ)||² and σ̂²=||y−μ(γ̂)||²/N; the optimized negative log-likelihood is constant+Nlnσ̂². [C.2, equations C.2.5–C.2.8, printed pp. 378–379; PDF pp. 398–399]
For a complex sinusoidal model with N_s samples and n_c components, the real data dimension is N=2N_s and parameter count is n=3n_c+1. [C.2, equations C.2.9–C.2.10, printed p. 379; PDF p. 399]

The MAP model-order rule selects the hypothesis maximizing p_n(y|H_n)p_n(H_n), reducing to maximum marginal likelihood under equal priors; it maximizes total probability of correct detection. [C.3.1, equations C.3.7–C.3.13, printed pp. 382–384; PDF pp. 402–404]

KL discrepancy D(p0,p̂)=E0[ln(p0/p̂)] is nonnegative and vanishes iff p̂=p0; minimizing it is equivalent to maximizing expected model log-likelihood. [C.3.2, equations C.3.15–C.3.19, printed pp. 384–385; PDF pp. 404–405]

Unpenalized maximized likelihood fails completely for nested order families because likelihood is monotone in order and always selects the maximum. The direct-KL ‘no-name’ correction adds penalty n, but still tends to overfit. [C.4, equations C.4.5–C.4.12, printed pp. 386–387; PDF pp. 406–407]

AIC minimizes −2ln p_n(y,θ̂_n)+2n. If a true finite order exists, its underfit probability tends to zero but its overfit probability tends to a positive constant; this same tendency can help approximation when all candidate models are misspecified. [C.5, equations C.5.8 and C.5.12–C.5.13, printed pp. 389–390; PDF pp. 409–410]

For linear regression, AICc replaces AIC’s penalty with [2N/(N−n−1)]n, reducing finite-sample overfit risk at some cost in underfit risk and converging to AIC as N grows. [C.5, equation C.5.15, printed pp. 390–391; PDF pp. 410–411]

With validation data ρ times longer than estimation data, GIC minimizes −2ln p_n(y,θ̂_n)+(1+ρ)n; ρ>1 selects no larger an order than AIC, but no universally optimal ρ exists. [C.6, equations C.6.1–C.6.5, printed pp. 391–392; PDF pp. 411–412]

Under standard information scaling, BIC minimizes −2ln p_n(y,θ̂_n)+nlnN and is asymptotically equivalent to the optimal MAP rule. If information components scale at different rates, the determinant scaling must be recomputed rather than applying nlnN blindly. [C.7, equations C.7.10–C.7.16, printed pp. 394–395; PDF pp. 414–415]
For sinusoids, the information determinant scales atypically and the BIC penalty becomes (5n_c+1)lnN_s, not the generic (3n_c+1)ln(2N_s). [C.7, equations C.7.13–C.7.14, printed p. 394; PDF p. 414]
If the data-generating mechanism is in the tested model class, BIC is consistent: its probability of selecting the correct order tends to one. [C.7, equation C.7.17, printed p. 395; PDF p. 415]

All four criteria share −2ln likelihood+η(n,N)n, with η=2 for AIC, 2N/(N−n−1) for AICc, ν for GIC, and lnN for BIC; the authors’ pragmatic ranking is BIC, GIC with ν=4, AICc, then AIC. [C.8.1, equations C.8.1–C.8.2 and Figure C.1, printed pp. 395–397; PDF pp. 415–417]

Multimodel inference can retain the M best orders and assign normalized weights proportional to exp[−XIC(n_k)/2], interpreting the information criterion as an estimate of twice the negative model log-likelihood. [C.8.2, equations C.8.3–C.8.6, printed pp. 397–398; PDF pp. 417–418]
pedagogy: This shard is a proof-oriented support layer for the main book. Appendix A starts from definitions and repeatedly turns them into reusable results with short constructive proofs; the emphasis is not broad linear-algebra coverage but precisely the range/null-space, eigenvalue, projection, conditioning, least-squares, and quadratic-minimization tools required by spectral and subspace methods. Appendix B changes register from deterministic matrix geometry to statistical limits: it motivates the CRB through spectral-error propagation, derives general and Gaussian formulas, then specializes them to the book’s three parametric settings. Importantly, the authors teach the limits of the tool alongside the formula—finite-sample unattainability, biased estimators, model-order uncertainty, and nuisance parameters that grow with sample size. Appendix C is a sustained derivation rather than a list of named criteria. MAP, KL discrepancy, cross-validation, and Laplace/Bayesian arguments each generate a penalty rule; the authors compare assumptions and failure modes before making a pragmatic recommendation. Sinusoidal estimation serves as a running worked specialization that forces careful counting of real parameters and information scaling. Proofs are generally algebraic, compact, and self-contained, with harder background results cited. Appendix D is deliberately terse and useful mainly as a check on selected exercises. The bibliography and subject-grouped references function as a research map: foundational, classical, and newer works are separated where that history helps. This range assumes advanced matrix algebra, multivariate calculus, probability densities, asymptotics, likelihood theory, and familiarity with the spectral models developed in Chapters 1–6; it contains no standalone exercise set beyond selected answers inherited from those chapters.

gems: The proof of |I−AB|=|I−BA| uses two three-factor block-matrix products whose left sides have the same determinant; the identity then immediately yields the shared nonzero eigenvalues of AB and BA. [A.3.1, Results R10–R11, printed p. 333; PDF p. 353]

The authors call best low-rank approximation a result that ‘even alone would be enough to make the SVD an essential matrix analysis tool,’ then prove it rather than merely cite Eckart–Young. [A.4, Result R18, printed pp. 339–341; PDF pp. 359–361]

A clean numerical warning turns an innocent formula into a practical lesson: evaluating LS through (A*A)^−1A* squares the condition number, so the mathematically correct normal equations can be computationally unwise. [A.8.2, printed p. 351; PDF p. 371]

LS and TLS are distinguished by a memorable modeling question: is only B noisy, or are both A and B perturbed? The two answers lead respectively to projection/QR and augmented-matrix SVD. [A.8.2, printed pp. 350–353; PDF pp. 370–373]
The CRB chapter begins by warning against ritual comparison: at small N the bound may be unattainable, and a biased estimator can have MSE below the unbiased CRB. [B.1, printed p. 356; PDF p. 376]

Unknown order has an explicit statistical price: average the conditional spectral bounds over the limiting order-selection probabilities, and the bound rises as the maximum candidate order expands. [B.1, printed pp. 357–358; PDF pp. 377–378]

The Gaussian CRB is framed as a broadly conservative benchmark: with matching mean/covariance, other distributions can carry extra exploitable information and therefore admit smaller bounds. [B.3, printed pp. 363–364; PDF pp. 383–384]

The array discussion shows a subtle failure of the familiar ‘ML attains CRB’ slogan: deterministic unknown snapshots add O(N) nuisance parameters, so the parameter-to-data ratio does not vanish. [B.6, printed pp. 373–374; PDF pp. 393–394]

After deriving deterministic and stochastic array models, the authors advise treating the assumptions as instruments for deriving algorithms, not as a metaphysical choice: use MLDet for simplicity or MLSto for greater accuracy regardless of the literal signal origin. [B.6, printed p. 376; PDF p. 396]

The unpenalized nested-model rule is not merely imperfect—it ‘fails completely’ by always choosing the maximum allowed order. This makes the need for information-criterion penalties unavoidable. [C.4, printed p. 386; PDF p. 406]

The first corrected KL penalty is deliberately called the ‘no-name’ rule. Its penalty n is enough to improve on raw likelihood but not enough to prevent overfitting, preparing the logic for AIC’s 2n. [C.4, printed pp. 386–387; PDF pp. 406–407]

AIC’s inconsistency is not presented as pure defect: when reality is more complex than every tested model, its willingness to select larger orders can improve approximation and prediction. [C.5, printed p. 390; PDF p. 410]

GIC gets an intuitive cross-validation story: make the validation sample longer than the estimation sample, and a model that learned the estimation noise has more opportunity to fail. [C.6, printed pp. 391–392; PDF pp. 411–412]

BIC’s claim to fundamentality comes from converging derivations: KL with an N-independent prior, full Bayesian marginal likelihood/MAP, and minimum description length all lead to the same logarithmic penalty form. [C.7, printed pp. 392–395; PDF pp. 412–415]

The sinusoid example catches a common plug-in error: Fisher information for frequency grows at a different rate, so generic nlnN parameter counting gives the wrong BIC penalty. [C.7, printed p. 394; PDF p. 414]
Figure C.1 makes the criteria’s personalities visible: AIC stays flat at 2, GIC ν=4 stays flat at 4, AICc falls toward 2, and BIC keeps growing as lnN. [C.8.1, Figure C.1, printed p. 397; PDF p. 417]

The final model-selection move avoids throwing away near-winners: exp(−XIC/2) converts criterion differences into normalized likelihood-style weights for a small ensemble. [C.8.2, printed pp. 397–398; PDF pp. 417–418]

One selected exercise answer gives a concrete warning that an ‘unbiased’ autocovariance sequence need not yield a nonnegative spectral estimate: y={1,1.1,1} produces a specified trigonometric estimate that can violate PSD validity. [Appendix D, answer 2.3, printed p. 399; PDF p. 419]

The reference apparatus is more than a bibliography: nonparametric, rational, line, and spatial literatures are split into historical/classical/recent strata, giving a ready-made research reading ladder. [References Grouped by Subject, printed pp. 415–419; PDF pp. 435–439]
